sections.body: Most account hacks don't need genius hackers. They use reused passwords, phishing and missing two-factor authentication.
Use a different strong password for every important account. A password manager can create and remember them. A long passphrase (4+ random words) is strong and memorable.

TWO-FACTOR AUTHENTICATION (2FA) adds a second step: something you have (an app code or security key) on top of something you know (your password). Even if your password leaks, the attacker usually can't log in.
PHISHING: fake messages that trick you into giving passwords or codes. Red flags: urgency, odd sender addresses, links to look-alike sites, requests for codes.
NEVER share a 2FA code. No real company will ask you for one. Set up recovery options (backup codes, a recovery email) before you need them.

quiz.q: Someone texts: 'I'm from support, I need the 6-digit code we just sent you to fix your account.' You should…
hints: Who should ever know your 2FA code?
Why would an attacker want the code?
A bank never asks for your PIN over the phone. 2FA codes are just as private.
quiz.explain: Never share a 2FA code. Real support teams will never ask for it. This is a classic account-takeover trick.

quiz.q: Why is reusing one password on many sites risky?
options: If one site leaks it, attackers try it everywhere
hints: What would an attacker do with a leaked password?
If one key opened your house, car and locker, losing it once would open everything.
quiz.explain: Leaked passwords get tried on other sites ('credential stuffing'). Unique passwords stop one leak spreading.

options: It needs something you have, not just something you know
hints: A password is something you know. The code comes from…?
A cash machine needs your card (have) AND your PIN (know). Why is that safer than a PIN alone?
quiz.explain: 2FA needs something you have (a phone or key) as well as your password, so a stolen password alone isn't enough.
